`@available` is a Swift compiler attribute that normally communicates platform/version availability (e.g. `@available(iOS 15, *)` marks something as introduced in iOS 15). The `unavailable` variant is a special case: instead of saying *when* something became available, it says the symbol can **never** be referenced from Swift source, on any platform — and the compiler enforces that as a hard error, not a warning.

Applied to the generated file, it'd look like:

```swift
@available(*, unavailable, message: "per-byte copy — use withUnsafePointerToPayload")
public var payload: FlatbufferVector<UInt8> { return _accessor.vector(at: VTOFFSET.payload.v, byteSize: 1) }
```

- `*` = applies to all platforms (as opposed to `iOS, unavailable` which would only block it on iOS).
- The property's body is untouched — it still compiles fine as a declaration. What changes is that **any code elsewhere that tries to write `typed.payload`** now fails to compile, with the custom message shown as the compiler error, pointing whoever hits it straight at `withUnsafePointerToPayload` instead.
- It does *not* delete or rename anything, which is why the Fable agent liked it here: it's a single line inserted above an otherwise-unmodified generated declaration, so it stays a tiny, obviously-correct diff against fresh `flatc` output — easy for a post-process script to reapply after every regeneration, and easy for a reviewer to spot if it's ever missing.
- It's stronger than `@available(*, deprecated, message: "...")`, which only produces a warning — warnings get ignored or suppressed. `unavailable` makes misuse structurally impossible rather than just discouraged, which is the actual goal here (closing the footgun, not just flagging it).

This is also how Apple's own SDKs commonly retire an API in favor of a new one — mark the old one `unavailable` (sometimes with `renamed:` to get an auto-fixit) so every call site is forced to migrate at compile time rather than relying on people noticing a warning.
and why do we need to put that?

Because without it, the exact same mistake is free to happen again, and nothing in the normal engineering loop would catch it before it ships:

1. **The bad call site looks completely idiomatic.** `Data(typed.payload)` reads like the obviously-correct way to turn a byte collection into `Data`. Nothing in the type signature (`FlatbufferVector<UInt8>: RandomAccessCollection`) hints that it's O(n) with a huge per-element constant factor instead of a bulk copy. A reviewer scanning the diff has no reason to flag it — it looks identical to the fast version at a glance.

2. **The failure mode is silent and delayed.** It doesn't crash. It doesn't fail a unit test — small test fixtures (a handful of notes) never have payloads big enough for the per-byte overhead to matter. It only shows up as "the app feels slow" after a real session with real data growth, which is exactly how you found it: by using the app, not by any test or CI signal. By the time a human notices, it's already in production-shaped usage.

3. **It's not a one-off risk.** The slow accessor is `public`, sits right next to the fast one, and gets regenerated fresh every time `flatc` runs. Any future call site — written by you, me, another agent, or a contributor who's never seen this bug — can reach for it again with zero warning.

4. **A written rule doesn't survive.** The obvious alternative is "remember not to do this" — a comment, a wiki note, a convention. But that only works if everyone who ever touches this code reads and recalls it, indefinitely. This codebase already has a working answer to that exact problem on the Rust side (the doctrine-lint "banned tokens" pattern) precisely because tribal knowledge decays and code review misses things — the fix is to make the mistake **structurally impossible** rather than merely discouraged.

5. **It's the cheapest possible guard.** One line, zero behavior change to anything currently working, and it converts an entire bug class from "silent runtime perf cliff that surfaces days later" into "red squiggly line the moment you type it." That's about as good a cost-to-leverage ratio as a fix gets.

So the annotation isn't decoration on top of the real fix — it *is* the durable part of the fix. The `withUnsafePointerToPayload` swap I made earlier only patches the one call site that already bit you; the `@available(*, unavailable)` annotation is what stops the next one from being written at all.
but is having that data payload with O(n) access still necessary/a good thing? or are we just addressing a symptom?

Good question — worth separating two different things that "O(n)" could mean here.

**The copy itself: legitimate, not a symptom.** A copy of n bytes is inherently O(n) — you can't do better than that if you actually need n bytes of independent data. And this payload genuinely needs to be independent: it gets handed off to `KernelModel+Apply.swift:39` and cached, potentially for a long time, across many future frames, until that projection changes again. If we *didn't* copy — kept a zero-copy slice pointing back into the original transport buffer instead — we'd have to keep that whole incoming frame's buffer alive for as long as any projection extracted from it stays cached. Given frames arrive ~4Hz and only some projections in each frame are cleared/superseded quickly, that trade would mean retaining large transport buffers indefinitely just to keep small cached slices alive — worse for memory on a mobile app than paying a small, bounded, per-projection copy up front. So no, the fact that it copies isn't the bug. What was wrong was *how* it copied: one byte at a time through Swift's generic `Sequence` machinery instead of a single hardware `memcpy`. That's a constant-factor problem, not a complexity problem — and the constant-factor difference is enormous (roughly what took CPU from 195%→0%). Fixing the constant factor was the correct target; you can't fix an asymptotic lower bound that isn't actually the bottleneck.

**Where there IS a legitimate "are we just addressing a symptom" angle:** `extractTypedProjections` eagerly copies out *every* typed projection's payload in *every* incoming frame, regardless of whether anything downstream currently cares about that particular projection this cycle. FlatBuffers' whole design premise — already leveraged elsewhere in this same file (`getRoot` unchecked, skipping the O(N) verifier walk) — is that you shouldn't have to touch/copy data you're not going to read. If most frames only have a handful of projections that anything is actually observing, and the rest get copied and then immediately discarded or overwritten, that's real wasted work at the complexity level (bytes copied that were never needed), not just a slow-constant-factor problem. Whether that's actually happening — i.e., whether frames typically carry a lot of "dead" projection payloads relative to what's consumed — I don't know yet; it depends on real frame composition and cache-hit patterns I haven't measured.

If you want, I can have an agent instrument or trace actual frame/projection cardinality (how many projections arrive per frame vs. how many are read by an active observer that cycle) to see if demand-driven/deferred decoding is worth pursuing as a follow-up, separate from today's fix. That would be a bigger design change, not a quick patch, so I'd want real numbers before recommending it.
